topic: DGX Spark vs Strix Halo: what the premium actually buys
title: DGX Spark vs Strix Halo: Speed Myth?
description: NVIDIA's DGX Spark packs up to one petaFLOP of FP4 compute at $6,950, while GMKtec's EVO-X3 with AMD Strix Halo and 128GB of shared memory sells for about $3,800. An owner's identical llama-bench runs on gpt-oss-120b tell a different story about token generation versus prompt processing. You'll learn what the Spark's premium actually buys and how to check your own workload against it. Which box would you pick? (Narration is AI-generated.)
hook_candidates: EVO-X3 or DGX Spark? One number decides.
You think $6,950 buys speed. It buys prompt processing.
Thirty-one hundred dollars apart. Same chat speed.
Same highway. Same speed. Different loading dock.
Forty-five percent cheaper. Same chat speed.
The $6,950 box is faster. Barely, where it counts.
One model fits both. One wallet disagrees.
The mini-PC that runs 120B like the Spark.
Same tokens per second. Very different receipts.
narration_full: You think six thousand nine hundred fifty buys speed. It buys prompt processing. You want one home box for giant open models. The spec sheet crowns the Spark. An owner benched both on one model. The Spark wrote fifty-six word-pieces a second, the mini-PC forty-seven. Writing rides on bandwidth, how fast weights stream. Two hundred fifty-six versus two hundred seventy-three gigabytes per second. Same doorway. Prefill, the pass reading your whole prompt, is one big math block, no doorway. There the Spark runs roughly two to five times faster. Giant prompts and agent loops earn the Spark. Everyday chat does not. Same chat speed, much faster prompt processing. That is the Spark's premium, three thousand one hundred dollars.

analogy.vehicle: A kitchen where the chef chops instantly but every ingredient arrives through one narrow doorway
analogy.mapping: The chef is compute, the Spark's petaFLOP; the doorway is memory bandwidth; the ingredients are the model's weights
analogy.limit: It breaks for prefill, which is one big block of math rather than one ingredient at a time, and that is exactly where the Spark's chef wins

notes_for_review: Rounded 56.33 and 47.46 tokens per second to fifty-six and forty-seven, kept the owner's prefill summary as 'roughly two to five times faster', and used the brief's own three-thousand-one-hundred-dollar gap; the hook price follows the assigned verbatim line with the dollar unit carried on screen as $6,950. Hedged the evidence as one owner's bench in narration and on screen ('One owner's run, not a lab'), and said 'mini-PC' rather than EVO-X3 because the benched box was an EVO-X2 with the same Strix Halo chip. The doorway analogy's limit lives in s05's clause 'one big math block, no doorway'.
